abstract: |
  A scientific study passes through many people, and each of them usually works with a different artifact. The study moves from the researcher to the ethics committee and the participant, and then on to the data engineer, the analyst, the reviewer, and the replicator. The artifact changes at each step: a protocol PDF and an experiment script become a preprocessing notebook, then a manuscript figure and a CONSORT diagram. Because these artifacts drift apart, no single representation describes the study as it was actually run. **Studyflow** is a visual notation that closes this gap by extending Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with elements specific to experimental cognitive sciences: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility criteria), data operations (map, filter, reduce), and data elements bound to community practices (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW). A single `.studyflow` file then serves as protocol, specification, publication figure, and participant-facing application. We describe the language, an open source modeler, and a runner. We then follow one reproducible study through its full lifecycle, from protocol design to publication: a battery of cognitive tasks administered to human participants and to artificial agents, and then compared across tasks, models, and demographics.
impact-statement: |
  Studyflow turns a scientific study into a single source-of-truth diagram that can be reviewed, executed, and published. It replaces the divergent artifacts that currently fragment experimental research across stakeholders, such as protocols, scripts, pipeline parameters, and diagrams.

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

A scientific study touches many people and systems. A researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it as a manuscript; and a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing the study later requires more than the data and the manuscript. It also requires an explicit and complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system needs both a data model (for its structure) and a process model (for its behavior) [@olive2007conceptual]. In cognitive sciences, however, most standardization has focused on the data, so the processes that produce the data are documented only in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift away from the text they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015].

The cost of this missing process model becomes clear whenever someone other than the author has to re-read a study. The researcher's protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card, the manuscript figure, and the CONSORT diagram all begin as different views of the same study, and they end as inconsistent ones. By that point, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Trust in research is built or lost at this point of divergence, and so is trust in the code and data on which research depends.

The usual way to make up for a missing process model is voluntary, narrative reporting, such as checklists, pre-registration forms, and journal endorsements. We now have evidence on whether this works. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that only 7%-14% had been preregistered and only 14%-16% shared raw data, despite more than a decade of reform initiatives [@hardwicke2024prevalence]. The pattern is not limited to psychology. ARRIVE 2.0 documents that endorsement by more than 1000 journals failed to improve adherence [@percie2020arrive], and a randomized controlled trial at *PLOS ONE* found that asking for a completed checklist at submission did not improve reporting compliance either [@hair2019iicarus]. Even at journals that have made transparency the default rather than an option, the change required explicit editorial mandates rather than voluntary uptake [@hardwicke2024transparency]. Narrative checklists are simply the wrong instrument, and this failure does not reflect uncooperative researchers. A checklist specifies *what to mention* without requiring *what to actually share*, and it accepts a narrative description of processes instead of a formal, verifiable one. The underlying process model therefore stays implicit and open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself, rather than separate documentation kept alongside the work. A single representation of a study that is machine-readable, human-understandable, and shared across its many audiences would force the process model and the data model to stay aligned. The contribution of this paper is one concrete version of that idea, built on a standard process notation and a working open-source tool that others can replace without losing the underlying specification.

## 1.2 Current practice fragments the study across artifacts

Today, each audience of science receives a different artifact, and each artifact drifts from the rest. We group current approaches into four overlapping families.

**Box-and-arrow figures** in manuscripts communicate study logic at a glance, but they are not standardized, not machine-verifiable, and rarely connected to the code that runs the study. Each one is tailored to a particular stakeholder: a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funding agency, or a sketch on a whiteboard for an engineer. This variety makes them hard to keep consistent with one another [@bogale2024]. **Checklists and pre-registration forms** are cataloged through the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator] and provide structured text. They store it, however, in free-form fields and in binary or proprietary formats such as PDF or DOCX, in data silos that resist version control. **Data standards, ontologies, and packages**, including BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, and CSVW [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw], make the data machine-readable, but they say little about the processes that produced it. Ontology-based process models are numerous, but they require high upfront effort and are rarely reused [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. **Code and configuration**, from analysis scripts, GitHub Actions, and Nextflow [@kinsman2021] to registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016], make pipelines precise. They require domain-specific programming skills, however, that exclude ethics boards, reviewers, and many collaborators.

The recurring pattern is a split between **execution** and **communication**. Tools that execute the study, such as scripts, workflow engines, and CI pipelines, are aimed at developers and machines. Tools that communicate the study, such as protocol PDFs, narrative platforms, and reporting checklists, are aimed at humans. Provenance systems track the computational graph well, but they rarely capture the full experimental context, such as randomization decisions, manual annotations, and protocol deviations. The result is a boundary between a well-tracked computational graph and a partially represented experimental graph [@souza2020provenance; @simmons2018provenance_sport]. No single representation currently spans the full lifecycle of a study in a form that scientists, engineers, funding agencies, ethics boards, and journal editors can all read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## 1.3 BPMN as a foundation

This domain covers the design, execution, and reporting of experiments in cognitive sciences. It meets the standard criteria for building a domain-specific modeling language (DSL): recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general-purpose code, and the absence of an executable language that already covers the whole experiment lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new graphical language for cognitive experiments, we extend an established one whose visual conventions are already used in other domains. The principles that separate an effective visual notation from a merely correct one are themselves a research topic [@moody2009physics]. A notation that researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is a cheaper starting point.

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature, ISO-standard graphical language for processes [@white2004introduction]. At the structural level it already provides what scientific workflows need: events, activities, sub-processes, decision making (gateways), data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography between participants. It has an established tooling ecosystem, with editors such as `bpmn-js` and Camunda Modeler, drawing libraries such as diagrams.net, and years of practice in industries where process clarity is essential. Building on BPMN gives any domain-specific extension a vocabulary that engineers and analysts already recognize, together with a standard serialization (BPMN 2.0 XML) that outlives any single tool.

We build on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms: `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes. The standard lets authors add domain-specific elements and attributes inside a new namespace, so a BPMN-only parser ignores them gracefully while a domain-aware tool can validate and render them [@magnani2009bpdmn]. BPMN extensions in other domains already show this pattern: BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless machine-learning pipelines [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], extensions for human-AI collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], and broader applications to healthcare [@pufahl2022]. A systematic review identifies dozens more profiles across domains [@zarour2019], and a related taxonomy classifies how such extensions relate to the BPMN core [@braun2014classification]. Cognitive and behavioral research is clearly missing from this list.

<!--
Recent large-language-model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

## 1.4 Contributions

We contribute five artifacts, each independently usable:

1. **A versioned language specification** for Studyflow, written as a LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that serves as the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules. LinkML is a schema-modeling framework that is increasingly used across biology, biomedicine, and ontology engineering, and it provides FAIR-aligned [@fair] serialization along with tools that generate documentation, a validator, and downstream converters. The Studyflow LinkML schema does not depend on any particular implementation, so a third party can target it directly without relying on the modeler's code.

2. **A layered set of runtime schemas** that mirror the LinkML specification in the YAML format that BPMN tooling reads. They consist of the language core, a companion cognitive layer, and four optional domain extensions: the Behaverse cognitive battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a large-scale data transformation layer, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking. New domain semantics plug in without changing the core.

3. **A library of worked example diagrams** that ship with the modeler, including a complete CONSORT 2025 randomized-trial template, a SPIRIT 2025 protocol schedule, and patterns for cognitive tasks, data collection, analysis pipelines, MLOps, multi-agent choreography, and reporting guidelines.

4. **The Studyflow Modeler**, an open-source client-side web application (MIT-licensed) for authoring, inspecting, simulating, validating, and publishing Studyflow diagrams. Its inspector and palette are generated from the schemas, so the language and the editor stay in sync.

5. **The Studyflow Runner**, a separate client-side application that parses, validates, and walks a Studyflow file step by step. It ships with built-in renderers for consents, instructions, questionnaire instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II), generic tasks, and embedded Behaverse cognitive-task runtimes; it supports seeded determinism for reproducible random branches; and it drives human participants, classic agents (via CogEnv), and language-model agents from the same diagram.

# 2. Results

Studyflow's working artifacts are a language, a modeler, and a runner. A single `.studyflow` source feeds all three and renders in three ways (Study, Gantt, Checklist) for different readers. We test them on one study: a battery of cognitive tasks administered to both human participants and a panel of artificial agents. Every stage of that study, from protocol to publication, reads and writes the same source, so the protocol an ethics board approves is the one participants run, the one the analysis uses, and the one the published figure comes from.

## 2.1 The Studyflow language

Studyflow is a domain-specific profile of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 [@white2004introduction], tailored to experimental research in cognitive sciences. We chose BPMN as the host notation, rather than inventing a new language, for three reasons. First, Studyflow diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, diagrams.net), while Studyflow-specific elements degrade gracefully. Second, BPMN's flowchart-like visual grammar is already familiar to many researchers, which lowers the barrier to adoption; readers new to flowcharts still face a learning curve, but a gentler one than a custom language would impose. Third, BPMN provides a formal extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) that adds domain semantics without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: start, end, intermediate, boundary, timer, and error *events*; tasks, sub-processes, and call activities; exclusive, parallel, inclusive, event-based, and complex *gateways*; sequence flows and message flows; data objects and data stores with their associations; pools and lanes; and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements use standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary that experimental research routinely needs. First, a top-level **study container** groups every other element and carries study-level metadata (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and the curated Behaverse cognitive battery); each one shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** add bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], the Behaverse Data Model, and CSVW) on top of BPMN's generic data objects, and a small **data-operations vocabulary** (map, filter, reduce, group, transform, and compose) shows the *kind* of transformation as a task marker, so the flow of data is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode the branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified-allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view can derive trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram.

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow does not redefine BPMN's serialization conventions, and it leaves XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base shape vocabulary untouched. Domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic BPMN renderer ignores them gracefully while a Studyflow-aware tool validates and renders them consistently.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is split into a small core and optional domain extensions that load on demand (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding (study container, events, sequence flows, base activity, data infrastructure) together with a companion cognitive layer (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest, video games, research gateways). Four optional layers cover specific domains: the Behaverse Unity battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking. New domains plug in by writing a schema, without changing the core. The complete element catalog is in Supplementary Table S1.

## 2.2 The Studyflow Modeler

The **Studyflow Modeler** is an open-source web application (MIT-licensed) that implements the Studyflow language for authoring, inspecting, simulating, and publishing diagrams. It runs entirely in the browser, with no server dependency. Two design choices shape the modeler. First, the language specification is kept as a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that is independent of the modeler codebase, so third-party tools (linters, converters, execution engines) can target the same specification; the modeler tracks the schema rather than owning it. Second, the user interface is **schema-driven**: the palette entries, the inspector panel, and the validation rules are all generated from the layered moddle schemas. Adding an element type or attribute to a schema updates the interface automatically, which keeps the modeler lightweight as the notation evolves with community feedback.

The authoring workflow (Figure 3) has seven steps. (1) **Sign in.** Users open the hosted modeler. A Behaverse API key unlocks publishing; guest mode supports draft-only authoring. (2) **Drag from the palette.** The left palette offers the BPMN base vocabulary alongside the Studyflow-specific elements (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction, random gateway, eligibility gateway, dataset, and so on); optional schemas can be turned on in the palette settings. (3) **Edit in the inspector.** Selecting an element opens a right-hand inspector sidebar whose fields come from the element's schema entry: required attributes are flagged, enumerated values become dropdowns, markdown fields show a preview, and conditional attributes appear only when their condition holds. (4) **Connect elements.** The connect tool wires sequence flows, data associations, and message flows, and it picks the right edge type from the source and target. (5) **Save and export.** Diagrams are saved as `.studyflow` files (BPMN 2.0 XML with Studyflow extensions in named namespaces), so they diff cleanly in Git and stay valid BPMN. Export to PNG and SVG produces publication-ready figures, and the SVGs can embed the source XML for one-file commits. (6) **Simulate.** A simulation mode steps through the diagram interactively, runs the gateway logic, and shows the next allowed elements, which helps catch dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs. (7) **Publish.** *File → Publish* uploads the diagram to the Behaverse Data Server [@bds], which builds its own participant-facing interface from the diagram structure (the local layout in the modeler is only for human readers, and the server ignores it). Local stimuli must be referenced by URL or uploaded separately. Each publish creates a new server-side version, so studies already in the field do not break when authors push updates, and earlier versions stay reachable by identifier.

This separation between the specification (the LinkML schema), the authoring tool (the modeler), the runtime interface (the data server), and the visual layout (export artifacts) lets each component evolve on its own, while a single `.studyflow` source ties them together.

## 2.3 The Studyflow Runner

The **Studyflow Runner** is a separate client-side application that takes a Studyflow diagram and walks a participant (or an artificial agent) through it node by node. It lives alongside the modeler. A diagram can reach it in three ways: from the modeler's *Run* button, through a URL parameter when the diagram is hosted somewhere, or by direct file upload. An optional random seed makes any branching deterministic, so pilot runs and regression tests are reproducible.

After loading, the runner parses the diagram, validates it node by node, and traverses it from start to end. Validation happens in layers. Type-level constraints (required attributes, enumerated values, conditional visibility) are checked at parse time; structural constraints (every start has an outgoing flow, every gateway is fully wired, every flow has a valid source and target) are checked by the modeler at edit time; and per-step validators (a questionnaire needs an instrument, a Behaverse cognitive task needs a paradigm identifier) run before traversal begins. The same per-step validators are also used by the modeler's lint pass, so authors see the errors they would see at run time. Each node the runner visits becomes a step that it renders and waits to complete; when the run reaches the end event, it finishes and applies any completion code or redirect the diagram specifies.

**Gateway semantics.** Random gateways pick an outgoing branch uniformly at random, controlled by the seed. Stratified allocation currently falls back to the same uniform pick; balanced stratification is left for future work. Exclusive and inclusive gateways evaluate conditions against a runtime variable store that nodes can write to as they run, and they fall back to a default branch when no condition matches. Parallel gateways are not yet supported.

**Built-in step kinds.** Six step kinds ship: a **start** node that shows a consent screen when one is attached, an **end** node that issues a completion code and an optional redirect, an **instruction** node that displays markdown, a **questionnaire** node with built-in instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, BDI-II) plus custom instruments defined by an inline schema, a **Behaverse cognitive-task** node that embeds the Behaverse Unity runtime and supports three response sources (Unity's in-game bot, runner-side uniform random, or a language-model call per trial), and a **generic-task** fallback. Elements that are not steps in the participant flow (data references, model-only sub-processes) are skipped at run time, because they matter for modeling and analysis rather than execution.

**Runtime extensibility.** New step kinds plug in by adding one folder to the runner's node directory: a small matcher selects which diagram elements the kind handles, a mapper extracts the runtime parameters from the element, and a React component renders the step. A domain group can therefore ship a custom step (an eye-tracking calibration, a VR scene) without forking the runner. The runner has a fixed set of step kinds, no parallel-gateway support, and a stratified-allocation fallback to uniform random. These are choices of scope rather than limits of the language, because the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and each gap corresponds to a roadmap item.

Figure 4 [GAP: a four-to-six-panel walkthrough of a participant moving from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a Behaverse cognitive task to the end screen, on the same diagram authored in §2.2.]

## 2.4 The three views: Study / Gantt / Checklist

A single `.studyflow` source can be rendered in three ways, each suited to a different stakeholder need (Figure 5). The three views read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph that shows every element and connection. The Study view is *structural*: it shows what happens and in what order, but it does not commit to wall-clock timing. It is the standard view for Methods sections, for reviewers checking the logical structure, and for pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering places time-sensitive elements along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress. Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on BPMN activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation is expressed directly as BPMN pools and lanes, which the Gantt uses to group rows; there is no separate `resourceAllocation` attribute. When these temporal attributes are present, the Gantt view renders the diagram automatically. The same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level timing (visit schedule, follow-ups). A milestone is simply an element with zero duration, and hierarchical Gantt structures map directly onto BPMN sub-processes. The Gantt view is useful for longitudinal studies and for SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of activities with their items and status. Every Studyflow element carries an optional `checklist` attribute (a markdown list) that the Checklist view extracts and aggregates. The view supports two uses: *running studies day-to-day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, CARE). For the second use, guideline items map to the diagram elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship with the `.studyflow` file and can be exported to JSON or Markdown for external task managers.

| If you need to communicate... | Use |
|---|---|
| Procedural structure, branching, data flow | Study view |
| Wall-clock timing, schedules, durations | Gantt view |
| Coverage against a reporting checklist or protocol | Checklist view |

A single `.studyflow` source therefore supports three ways of reading it (a methods diagram, a project schedule, and a reporting audit), without forcing authors to maintain three separate artifacts that drift apart.


## 2.5 Design: the protocol, randomization, and reporting scaffolding

Our worked example is a single study that administers a battery of cognitive tasks to human participants and a panel of artificial agents, and then compares them across tasks. We design it as a randomized controlled trial. The protocol then carries the scaffolding a registered study needs: consent, eligibility screening, random allocation to two groups (a self-paced group and a time-pressured group), task order counterbalanced within each group, and the structure a journal will later expect. In current practice this scaffolding is spread across a registry entry, an ethics PDF, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up time. None of these is a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort]. The flow diagram, in particular, is a participant-tracking schematic; its four standard rows are enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis, and attrition counts annotate each transition. It is a *document* about the trial, and it is not the *spec* that drove it. Studyflow makes the document and the spec one file.

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram that ships with the modeler; authors can fork it, parameterize it, and run it as the actual protocol of a new trial [@hopewell2025consort]. Figure 6 compares three artifacts: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text-and-box treatment.

The key mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation that sits next to the column of follow-up activities, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an error end event with a labeled count. This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the trial's topology, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, rather than an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Second, summing attrition becomes a graph operation instead of a manual exercise, so a Studyflow-aware validator can check that no row's outbound counts exceed its inbound count. Third, the boundary error event is the same primitive that BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram stays valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@stroppi2011; @ait2024bpmn_humanagent].

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references a participant-facing consent PDF, so a runner that reaches this node renders the consent screen automatically, before any randomization happens. The screening task carries a markdown checklist (demographic intake, medical history, baseline cognitive screen) that also drives the Checklist view. The eligibility gateway and the randomization gateway are typed as such, and each task in the battery declares itself as a cognitive task with its own inline parameter block (for the n-back: the N level, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block). The allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks each carry their own checklists that describe protocol obligations. A single file therefore serves four readers at once: the trial registry (a registered protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria), the ethics board (consent content and per-task checklists), the data-collection platform (the embedded cognitive-task instrument and its parameters), and the journal (the CONSORT figure with attrition flows already wired). The mechanism is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011]: each reader interprets the layer it cares about. What is new is that the union of those layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, based on a worked SPIRIT template that the modeler ships. Its 34 checklist items across 9 topics map onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events once the study has run.

## 2.6 Collect: one diagram, many executors

Data collection makes Studyflow's central idea concrete: *who executes the protocol is a runtime decision rather than a property of the diagram*. Our study administers a six-task battery drawn from the Behaverse suite, spanning working memory (n-back and digit span), attention (multiple-object tracking), processing speed (pattern comparison), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning), and set-shifting (card sorting). One `.studyflow` source drives every task and every executor. The n-back serves as the worked example below, a near-universal probe of working memory [@owen2005nback], and the other five use the same machinery.

**The round-trip.** We built the battery in the Studyflow Modeler and saved it as one Studyflow diagram. This single source orchestrates consent, baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to two groups (self-paced and time-pressured), and a sequence of the six tasks. Each task sits in the diagram as a Behaverse cognitive-task node, and task order is counterbalanced within each group. We then loaded that file into the Studyflow Runner. Each task is itself a Behaverse timeline of blocks: a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase. The battery is therefore a nested structure that prose and slides flatten but the diagram keeps explicit. The runner checks that every task's required parameters are present before traversal begins, and then walks the diagram one node at a time (Figure 4). Instructions are shown as markdown, the questionnaire before the task uses a built-in instrument (PHQ-9, GAD-7, and BDI-II all ship, and custom instruments are accepted through an inline schema), and trial-level execution is handed to the Behaverse Unity runtime through the Behaverse cognitive-task node. Seeded randomization, set as a URL parameter (`?seed=42`), makes the within-task sequence and every random branch deterministic. This is what lets a pilot dataset be reproduced exactly from the same source.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 7 places the traditional slide-style N-back figure next to the Studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the boundary between trial and block stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow instead encodes the trial as an explicit subgraph, built from a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second boundary timer for the inter-trial interval, and text annotations that label the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is illustrative. For runs beyond a handful of trials, the same logic compresses into a single Behaverse cognitive task. Its inline configuration declares the N level, stream specification, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval, and the runner expands it into individual trials through the Behaverse Unity runtime. The XML excerpt in Figure 7c shows how these primitives are serialized. The same compression applies to every task in the battery: each one is a Behaverse cognitive-task node whose inline timeline, blocks, stop rules, and optional staircase the runtime expands into trials. Each trial the runner emits is logged to the Behaverse Data Model trials-level schema [@bdm], which is Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds], so the same diagram produces a CSV whose columns are fixed by the schema and whose meaning is fixed by the diagram, identically across all six tasks. The trials CSV can be reviewed side by side with the diagram, and a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without running the modeler.

**Three kinds of executor.** The same source reaches three runtimes today. Each uses a different adapter, and all of them emit trials under the common schema (Figure 12). *Human participants* run through the Behaverse Data Server: the author publishes the diagram, the server builds its own participant-facing interface from the diagram structure, and the trials are logged under the schema. *Classic reinforcement-learning agents* run through CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], which administers Behaverse cognitive tasks to RL policies through DeepMind's AndroidEnv layer and exposes them to the same screenshots, response buttons, and time constraints a human would see. Running a random or scripted policy through every node also serves as protocol validation, since it reveals stuck states and timing edge cases before any human sits down. *Language-model agents* run through the runner's per-trial bridge: each trial is sent to the configured model with a free-form prompt that steers a simulated participant (trait, target accuracy, mistake rate). Vision-capable models read the on-screen frame through an optional screenshot pathway, so the battery's spatial tasks (object tracking, matrix reasoning, card sorting), which carry no useful textual stimulus, stay tractable. If a model returns an answer outside the allowed set, the runner records the mismatch and falls back to a uniform random choice, so a transient failure cannot silently corrupt the dataset.

**Profiling a panel of agents.** Because the executor is a parameter, we profile a matrix of agents against the whole battery, rather than scoring one agent on one task. We cross three factors: *model* (a uniform-random baseline, a commercial vision-language model, and an open-weight model served locally for offline and HPC-side use), *trait* (a careful "expert" aiming for near-ceiling accuracy, a "tired" participant aiming for roughly 80%, and a "fast-guesser" that trades accuracy for speed), and *task* (the six battery tasks). A trait prompt fixes the participant's character, whether the careful expert, the tired participant, or the fast-guesser, and it stays the same across the whole battery. Each task then supplies its own response instructions (reply Match or NonMatch for the n-back, Same or Different for pattern comparison, the option label for matrix reasoning, and so on), so each model produces a profile across constructs rather than a single score. We piloted every model-by-trait-by-task cell for [N] trials at seed 42, with no edits to the source diagram between runs (Figure 13, Table 3). The table reports accuracy, median response time, and the rate at which a reply fell outside the allowed set and triggered the runner's random fallback. The random baseline sits near chance on every task. The trait prompts move the commercial model toward their accuracy targets, both on the tasks that allow a textual reading and, through the screenshot pathway, on the spatial tasks that have no textual stimulus at all. The open-weight model follows the same profile, at some cost in accuracy, while running without an external API. The comparison therefore yields a profile across constructs rather than a single scalar score. It shows how faithfully each model holds a trait across constructs, how its accuracy and response-time ordering over tasks compares with the human ordering, and where open- and closed-weight models diverge, all from one diagram and all collected into one table whose columns are fixed by the schema rather than by which executor produced the row. This is the "few models, many items" regime [@ansarinia2022cogenv], made tractable and extended across tasks: where past work would rank many models on a single task, we vary the diagram (task, difficulty, response window, trait) and profile a handful of agents over a whole battery of parametrically related items.

**Beyond one participant.** The battery is administered to one participant at a time, but the same notation also scales to designs where the *interaction itself* is the unit of analysis. Joint action has been a central concern in cognitive science for two decades [@sebanz2006joint], supported by dyadic decision experiments, parent-child protocols, two-player games, and hyperscanning paradigms that measure neural coupling between simultaneously recorded participants [@babiloni2014hyperscanning; @hakim2023interbrain]. BPMN 2.0's **choreography task** models exactly this: a directed exchange between participants with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography]. Studyflow inherits it unchanged for dyadic, experimenter-driven, and parent-child patterns. Synchronization across instruments, rather than across people, is handled one layer down by the Lab Streaming Layer, the de facto architecture for collecting timestamped multimodal streams across heterogeneous devices [@kothe2025lsl]. A Studyflow diagram declares which actors interact and in what order, while LSL aligns the EEG, eye-tracker, and behavioral streams it references through schema-bound datasets.

**Beyond human participants.** The artificial-agent panel above is the same construct seen from a different angle. Confederate paradigms, in which a hidden agent stands in for a participant, have shaped cognitive science for decades [@dahlback1993woz]. That role is now routinely filled by language models: they are used to simulate participants and replicate published effects at scale [@aher2023llms], evaluated as cognitive subjects in their own right [@binz2023gpt3], or set up as generative confederates in richer environments [@park2023agents]. A choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans. As LLM-driven discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories that propose, execute, and interpret experiments end-to-end [@ghareeb2025], the case for an explicit, machine-readable procedural specification only grows. The runner does not yet traverse choreography tasks (a roadmap item), but the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema [@stroppi2011].

**Honest limits.** The multi-executor setup works today for the curated Behaverse battery: the six tasks used here, plus sustained attention, useful-field-of-view, spatial cueing, simple reaction time, and others, 22 in total. This works because those tasks ship as Unity scenes that the Behaverse Data Server, CogEnv, and the runner all recognize. A custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych task referenced from a Studyflow diagram can still be run for human participants, but the RL and LLM adapters would need a matching bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. Studyflow is also not a stimulus-presentation library: rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the Behaverse Unity runtime or an external framework reached by URL. The diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record; the pixel-level mechanics of showing it are left to the runtime. Generalizing the trial-level interface beyond Behaverse Unity is a roadmap item.

## 2.7 Analyze and compare: a reproducible pipeline over human and agent trials

In the analysis stage, the dominant artifact is a script: an R or Python notebook with implicit dependencies, comments instead of types, and no machine-readable record of its steps. Studyflow's data operations give every script-style operation an explicit type (element-wise map, row filter, partition group, group-wise reduce, expansion, generic transform, and bundled pipeline), so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram rather than buried in code. Together with dataset, data-store, and schema elements, the diagram becomes a complete, machine-readable pre-registration of the analysis.

We analyze the trials collected above through a nine-step pipeline. First, read the raw trials from the dataset the runner emitted. Second, filter invalid trials (RT < 100 ms, missing data, fallback-flagged rows). Third, map to derived measures (log-RT, accuracy, per-task correctness codes). Fourth, branch at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest (here, task, executor, and trait). Fifth, group by task, executor, and trait. Sixth, reduce to per-group accuracy, median RT, and standard errors. Seventh, route through a manual review where the analyst inspects outliers and optionally re-runs with adjusted criteria. Eighth, render the figures through a script task that plots accuracy and response time by task, group, and trait. Ninth, write the summary table and the figures, each to a schema-declared dataset. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if`; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema on the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

The same diagram carries process and data together, which is what makes the human-versus-agent comparison auditable. Most workflow tools separate the *process* (what runs, and in what order) from the *data* (the tables, columns, and units it consumes and produces): UML splits them into activity and class diagrams [@cuevasvicenttin2013workflows], DAG engines describe the process in code and leave data layout to convention, and reporting guidelines describe the process in prose and the data in a separate file. Studyflow puts both on one canvas. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph, while datasets, stores, catalogs, schemas, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph; BPMN data associations, drawn as dashed edges, connect the two. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], while non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and the Behaverse Data Model [@bdm] are typed contracts that the modeler validates and the runner respects, rather than comments, so an analyst can confirm from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Figure 8 shows the RT-analysis subprocess beside the equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline a tidyverse user would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, but it adds two commitments. First, the inputs and outputs are typed: the raw and summary datasets are typed (BDM trials level on the way in, models level on the way out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches an undeclared column or runs an unauthorized operation. The comparison this produces is the one that data collection set up: accuracy and response-time distributions across task, executor, and trait, shown side by side and reproducible from the seed. When human pilot data is collected, the human arm slots into the same table and schema the agents wrote to.

Pre-registration of analysis then becomes the diagram itself. In current practice, a pre-registered plan is free text on a registry website, with no machine-checkable link to the code that is eventually run. Under the Studyflow encoding, the diagram is the spec and the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation; any divergence between the two can be detected by inspecting the data-operation markers and the input and output schemas. We have not yet measured how legible large process-plus-data diagrams are, compared with the artifacts they replace. The modeler reduces visual density with collapsible layers: the high-level protocol turns the data layer off, and the full dependency graph turns it on. We leave the legibility question itself for future readability studies.

[GAP: the worked RT dataset for Figure 8. The model-by-trait-by-task agent-panel pilot (seed 42) is the reproducible anchor; a human battery RT dataset can slot into the same schema when available.]

## 2.8 Model: a machine-learning pipeline in the same notation

The analysis stops at group summaries, but the same trials can feed a model: a classifier of human versus agent, a model of the response-time distribution across tasks and difficulty levels, or, with accompanying neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. ML pipelines face the same fragmentation that experimental protocols do: the model card lives in one repository, feature engineering in another, the training script in a third, the deployment config in a fourth, and retraining triggers in cron jobs that nobody can find, if they exist at all. Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and schema-bound data elements apply to ML pipelines as cleanly as to behavioral analyses; within a Studyflow, an analysis and a training pipeline share one notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

The most demanding case is a multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline that would harmonize EEG, fMRI, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets. This pipeline is forthcoming; the encoding here is the Studyflow diagram that would specify it (Figure 11). It specializes the generic process-orchestration and data-transformation layers with concrete neuroimaging primitives. Modality-specific preprocessing for fMRI and EEG runs as parallel subprocesses. Behavioral data is converted to BDM trials [@defossez2020bdm], the same schema the battery's agents wrote to. Three properties then become explicit that are hard to recover from prose. First, **provenance is the diagram**: every derived artifact traces back to its raw source through the nodes that produced it. Second, **multiverse is first-class**: the multiple defensible analytical paths at each step are explicit branches rather than version-controlled forks of a script. Disagreement between pipelines then becomes a structured comparison [@steegen2016multiverse]. Third, **cross-dataset interoperability is a schema decision**: a preprocessing subprocess defined once applies to every dataset whose recordings follow the same format. The same encoding extends to containerized execution on an HPC cluster, and to downstream model-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, and monitoring subprocesses [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml]. Planned data-governance operations would make regulatory steps first-class diagram elements rather than annotations [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health].

## 2.9 Report and publish: one file against the publication guidelines

The lifecycle closes where it began, with the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. Because the study ran inside the same file, the CONSORT figure is not redrawn at write-up time; the modeler exports it from the protocol that ran the trial, with the attrition counts already written into the boundary error events. The figure that appears in the paper is the file that ran the study. This is the most direct answer to the "different artifacts drift" problem that motivates this work.

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for, rather than a PDF assembled alongside it. Each guideline is, in structure, a controlled vocabulary, a checklist, and sometimes a flow diagram, and Studyflow handles all of them in the same way: checklist items become entries in the optional `checklist` attribute on the relevant element, flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition where applicable, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view shows the items as a markdown list, with each one linked back to the element that satisfies it, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. The EQUATOR network catalogs these standards [@simera2010equator]; Table 2 lists the eleven most widely used, together with Studyflow's current coverage.

| Topic | Guideline | Template ships? | Checklist view? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Randomized trials | CONSORT | Yes | Yes |
| Study protocols | SPIRIT | Yes | Yes |
| Observational studies | STROBE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Systematic reviews | PRISMA | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Diagnostic/prognostic | STARD | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Case reports | CARE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Clinical practice | AGREE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Qualitative research | SRQR | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Animal pre-clinical | ARRIVE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Quality improvement | SQUIRE | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |
| Economic evaluations | CHEERS | [GAP, small] | [GAP, small] |

Two guidelines ship as worked templates today: CONSORT 2025 and SPIRIT 2025. CONSORT 2025's 30-item checklist [@hopewell2025consort] maps onto the shipped CONSORT template, and SPIRIT 2025's 34 items across 9 topics [@chan2025spirit] map onto a Gantt view (Figure 9) that serves as both the study schedule and the SPIRIT checklist. The other nine are roadmap items rather than gaps in the mechanism: the elements, attributes, and Checklist view are already in place, and each remaining guideline takes roughly half a day of authoring, with STROBE and PRISMA next. The pattern recurs across the catalog. PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study-flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes. TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes participant-facing intervention details first-class items that map almost line by line onto the participant branch. And ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], whose history of endorsement without adherence is itself one of the strongest arguments for an executable backbone, supplies the animal-research counterpart.

The deeper point is that reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. A SPIRIT protocol is a *plan* and a CONSORT diagram is a *report*; in current practice the two are written by different people, at different times, into different files. Encoded as a Studyflow, they become the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts afterward. At publication, the manuscript ships three artifacts that are all views of one source: the exported figure, the Checklist-view audit against the target guideline, and the `.studyflow` file itself, paired with the schema-conformant trials table. From these, a reader can reconstruct what every element and every column means, without rerunning the study.

---

# 3. Discussion

## 3.1 What Studyflow changes

Current practice keeps the *protocol*, the *pipeline*, and the *figure* as three separate artifacts. They begin in agreement, and over a project's life they drift apart. Studyflow consolidates these into a single source-of-truth file. One CONSORT diagram is, at the same time, the participant-flow figure, the spec a reviewer audits against the checklist, and the runnable artifact that the runner steps through. The battery is the protocol text, the trial-loop logic, and the executable tasks. The response time pipeline is both the analysis section and the transformation script. Because there is only one source, these views can no longer drift apart. This consolidation brings several advantages:

1. **Stakeholder alignment from a single source.** An ethics reviewer, a collaborator, and an engineer all read the same diagram, each at a different zoom level: the Study view for procedural structure, the Gantt for timing, and the Checklist for guideline compliance. They no longer work from three documents whose details disagree subtly.

2. **Versionable, reviewable artifacts.** A Studyflow file is plain BPMN 2.0 XML with stable identifiers, so it diffs cleanly in Git and embeds inside an SVG export. The figure in the manuscript thus carries its own machine-readable source. Procedural specifications come under the same review and version-control discipline that already governs data and code.

3. **Reusability through specification independence.** The language is maintained as a LinkML schema, independently of the modeler. Third-party tools such as linters, converters, and alternative renderers can therefore target the specification directly, without depending on any single application.

4. **Process and data on one diagram.** Data artifacts (datasets, tables, schemas, snapshots) and data operations (map, filter, reduce, group) live alongside the procedure that produced them. Community-schema bindings (BIDS, Psych-DS, BDM, CSVW) then attach to specific tasks, and each binding survives review.

5. **Reporting-guideline conformance becomes a diagram property.** Checklist items, vocabulary, and flow diagrams from reporting guidelines such as CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and PRISMA map directly to elements of the diagram. Conformance is therefore checkable in the source file itself and needs no parallel PDF.

6. **One protocol, many executors.** The same source runs human participants, classic reinforcement-learning agents, and language-model agents through different runtime adapters. Benchmarks for AI systems no longer need to be written three times in three different formats. The protocol stays one artifact, and its execution is a runtime decision.

The claim underlying all six is **trust by construction**: reproducibility lives in the shared artifact itself, with no reliance on add-on documentation. The diagram an ethics board approved is the diagram the participants ran, and it is the diagram the figures were generated from. That guarantee is stronger than current practice offers. On that basis, we expect Studyflow to compose with existing reproducibility infrastructure rather than compete against it.

## 3.2 Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of four ecosystems, and it does not aim to replace any of them.

**Execution stacks.** A whole family of engines solves a problem that Studyflow leaves alone: scalable and reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute. These include Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, and domain-specific engines such as NiPype and Pydra [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Their representations target machines and developers; ethics boards and journal reviewers fall outside that audience. A more basic limitation runs through all of them: they rely on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) as their underlying computational model. DAGs suit data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs. Scientific inquiry, by contrast, is inherently iterative: hypothesis generation, experimentation, and revisited analysis form continuous feedback loops, which AI-driven discovery systems are beginning to put into practice [@ghareeb2025]. BPMN expresses these cycles natively, through its sequence flows, boundary events, and choreography; a DAG-based stack must emulate them through external control logic or repeated workflow executions. Studyflow sits *above* such systems: a Studyflow task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, or a NiPype workflow), and a downstream tool can compile the protocol-level diagram into an executable graph for one of these engines. The boundary is deliberate: we prioritize communication over execution [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. By the same logic, Studyflow leaves process-mining and post-hoc conformance analysis on runtime traces to other tools; those traces still conform to a structure that downstream process-mining tools can consume directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Data standards.** BIDS, Psych-DS, the Behaverse Data Model, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured, but they say nothing about the process that produced them [@bids; @psychds; @bdm; @csvw]. Studyflow describes that process and references the data standards through schema-bound dataset, table, and schema elements. The two are complementary: a Studyflow diagram with a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells both the reader and the machine *what* was collected and *how*.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and STARD, together with their siblings, enforce structure at the publication stage [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard]. Today, conformance is checked by hand against PDF supplementary materials. Studyflow can carry these guidelines: a CONSORT diagram authored as Studyflow carries the checklist items as elements, and the same idea applies to SPIRIT. Conformance then becomes a property the diagram can be checked against, built into the structure rather than added later as a checklist.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human-agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains. Studyflow's layered schema architecture follows the same pattern: a core, a companion cognitive layer, and four optional domain layers. We expect future extensions for neuroimaging, clinical neurology, or developmental research to layer in the same way, without modifying the core. Visual modeling languages already used in life-sciences-adjacent fields, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

Studyflow is also not an ontology of experimental design. Process ontologies are numerous, but they tend to have high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. We have aimed instead for a profile small enough to learn from one worked example and a glossary, and enforced by tooling rather than by inspection.

Across these four ecosystems, a shared architectural pattern makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] share one pattern but occupy *different planes* of it. The pattern has a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and one or more machine-readable outputs, and each system covers a different aspect of a study: LinkML over the data model, NIDM-Results over analysis outputs, BIDS over multimodal data organization, and ARTEM-IS over methods reporting. The procedural plane of this pattern, an end-to-end, machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap that Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG-methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON. Studyflow generalizes the same commitment, from EEG-methods reporting to whole-study procedural specification. Concrete interoperability follows naturally from this framing: Studyflow diagrams can emit NIDM-Results-compatible analysis sub-graphs, schema-bind `Dataset` elements to BIDS layouts, express their data plane in LinkML, and export their methods-reporting block as ARTEM-IS-compatible JSON. None of these crosswalks subsumes a neighbor; the value is mutual.

## 3.3 Future directions

The language and tooling leave room to grow, and the layered design keeps each addition incremental. On the data side, the vocabulary could gain timeseries and event-marker structures, storage and data-governance operations, and a broader tidyverse-style operator set. On the tooling side, a data-store schema editor, richer inspector ergonomics, and further worked examples sit on the roadmap. Runner support for parallel gateways, stratified allocation, and choreography traversal is also planned. In time this could let a diagram drive downstream execution stacks such as Kedro, Nextflow, or NiPype. We describe these as open directions; none has shipped yet.

Some experimental designs are intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs. Adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs need representations of feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay loops. These demands exceed what BPMN sequence flow encodes naturally. The choreography and message-flow elements can express some of this; the rest is current research.

A larger question is community formation. Sibling BPMN profiles in clinical pathways and serverless ML emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation. Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap, each one being a single schema file plus optional renderer code. Adoption beyond our group is still limited. We have tried to lower the bar. The tool ships MIT-licensed and browser-only, with BPMN 2.0 XML on disk, LinkML as the source of truth, and no server dependency. The bar exists nonetheless. External adoption signals are the goal. We look for forks of the modeler for adjacent domains and for third-party validators against the LinkML schema. We also look for re-use of the SPIRIT and CONSORT templates in registered reports and journal supplements. [GAP: community-adoption signals (fork counts, external data-server deployments, or third-party Studyflow files in the wild) to be added when available.]

Two lines of empirical work would strengthen the evidence base. The first is a readability and comprehension study with 5-10 cognitive scientists. It would compare Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace: protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts. This tests the *trust by construction* claim against measured reviewer effort. The second is a set of end-to-end demonstrations beyond the single study reported here: a multi-session longitudinal study, an ABAB single-subject design, and an MLOps pipeline with a fairness audit and retraining loop. Each one would map the boundaries of what the current vocabulary covers. Both are realistic for a follow-up applications paper once Studyflow has been picked up by groups outside our own.

# Code and data availability


All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The hosted modeler is at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app>, the hosted runner at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/run.html>, and the documentation at <https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/docs/>. The modeler, runner, runtime schemas, example diagrams, and documentation all live in `github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler`, and the canonical LinkML schema is versioned separately at `github.com/behaverse/schemas`.

The versions used in this paper are tagged in the repository, and a stable release will be tagged at camera-ready time. End-to-end tests cover the create / inspect / save / load / run round-trip for each example diagram.

Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and three agent-profiling demos (`bot_external.studyflow`, a randomized baseline; `bot_claude.studyflow`, a commercial language model; and `bot_ollama.studyflow`, a local open-weight model). Reproducing every figure requires opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG. Runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner with seed 42. Permanent links to the exact source commits will be added to the camera-ready version.
